title: Portfolio and order pages slow, users logged out
outcome_reasons: the leading hypothesis has confidence 0.35, below 0.5
HYP-1 and HYP-2 are too close to tell apart
summary: Around 10:12‑10:14 UTC the postgres‑orders database saturated (CPU ~100%, connections >2× baseline, query latency >60×). The dominant workload was a simple SELECT on positions executed >1k times per minute. This caused portfolio‑service timeouts and p99 latency >2.5 s, and auth‑service session loss because its Redis cache became unavailable. A config reload at 09:31:44 that doubled work_mem (chg:2519) may have contributed, but a sudden surge of concurrent reads, a missing index, or a Redis degradation are also plausible. Evidence is insufficient to single out one root cause.

hypothesis.mechanism: Increasing work_mem doubled per‑query memory allocation; with many concurrent executions the instance ran out of memory, causing CPU thrashing, connection‑slot exhaustion and query timeouts.
predictions: Reverting work_mem to 4 MB should reduce CPU and connection pressure quickly.
pg_stat_statements will show high memory‑grant usage for the positions query.

hypothesis.mechanism: An unexpected burst of concurrent SELECT * FROM positions (e.g., a batch job or feature flag) saturated CPU and connection pool, leading to timeouts and downstream latency.
predictions: orders‑service or a scheduler will show a spike in request rate at ~10:12.
Connection count correlates with incoming request rate.

hypothesis.mechanism: Missing or ineffective index on positions.account_id forces full‑table scans; each scan consumes CPU and holds connections longer, producing the observed overload.
predictions: EXPLAIN ANALYZE will show a Seq Scan on positions.
Creating the index will drop query latency dramatically.

hypothesis.mechanism: Redis memory pressure or restart caused mass eviction of portfolio position caches and auth sessions; services fell back to postgres‑orders (cache miss storm) and forced re‑logins, overloading the DB.
predictions: Redis metrics will show a sharp memory‑usage drop or eviction spike at ~10:12.
Redis logs will show a restart or OOM event.

facts.statement: postgres‑orders CPU utilisation rose from baseline 0.34 to 0.95 by 10:40 UTC, first high point ~10:14.
Active connections on postgres‑orders climbed from baseline ~73 to 175 at 10:40 UTC.
Query latency p99 on postgres‑orders jumped from baseline ~18 ms to 1067 ms by 10:40 UTC, first rise ~10:14.
Postgres log shows 1050 executions of ‘SELECT * FROM positions WHERE account_id = $1’ between 10:14:01 and 10:39:59.
Postgres log reports 302 ‘FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for non‑replication superuser connections’ errors starting 10:16:25.
Checkpoint frequency warnings appeared at 09:33 and 10:25.
Config change chg:2519 at 09:31:44 raised work_mem from 4 MB to 8 MB (reload).
portfolio‑service latency p99 rose from baseline 424 ms to 2780 ms at 10:40 UTC, first rise ~10:13.
portfolio‑service error rate increased from baseline 0.002 to 0.048 at 10:40 UTC.
Portfolio logs show 1604 cache‑misses for positions loading from postgres‑orders starting 10:13:01.
Portfolio logs show 496 query‑timeout errors (2000 ms) to postgres‑orders starting 10:16:01.
auth‑service logs 665 ‘session not found in redis; forcing re‑login’ events starting 10:12:36.
Dependency graph: portfolio‑service → postgres‑orders (hard, 2000 ms) and → redis‑cache (soft, 100 ms).

assumptions.statement: The work_mem reload took effect immediately and remained at 8 MB for the incident window.
assumptions.reason: Config change was a reload; no further changes recorded.

assumptions.statement: The dominant SELECT on positions uses work_mem (e.g., large sorts or hash aggregates).
assumptions.reason: Higher work_mem only impacts operators that allocate memory.

assumptions.statement: A surge of concurrent positions reads originated upstream (batch job or feature flag) not captured in change history.
assumptions.reason: No deploy or config change on callers observed; connection count rose sharply.

assumptions.statement: Planner may have chosen a sequential scan on positions because statistics were stale or table grew past a threshold.
assumptions.reason: Missing index would cause full scans; no schema change recorded.

assumptions.statement: Redis cache experienced memory pressure or a brief restart around 10:12, causing evictions and session loss.
assumptions.reason: Simultaneous cache‑miss storm in portfolio and session loss in auth point to a common Redis issue, but no Redis telemetry was collected.

gaps.scope: redis-cache CPU, memory, eviction rate, uptime 09:30‑10:40
gaps.reason: Redis telemetry not queried; needed to confirm or reject H4.
No Redis logs retrieved; would show restarts or OOM.

gaps.scope: orders-service request rate, error rate, latency 09:30‑10:40

gaps.reason: Could reveal batch job or feature‑flag activation.

gaps.scope: postgres-orders EXPLAIN ANALYZE for the positions query
gaps.reason: Plan details missing; needed to test H1 vs H3.

actions.description: Collect Redis metrics (memory, evictions, uptime) and logs for 09:30‑10:40.
Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for SELECT * FROM positions WHERE account_id = $1 on a replica.
actions.rationale: Determines index usage and memory‑grant behavior (H1 vs H3).

actions.description: Revert work_mem to 4 MB via ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem='4MB'; SELECT pg_reload_conf();
actions.rationale: If config change (H1) is contributing, this reduces per‑query memory pressure quickly.

actions.description: Enable pg_stat_statements snapshot for last 30 min and capture top‑SQL.
actions.rationale: Quantifies query load to validate capacity‑saturation (H2) or missing index (H3).

actions.description: Review orders‑service request rate and any scheduled batch jobs around 10:12.
If index missing, create CREATE INDEX ON positions(account_id); if connection slots exhausted, raise max_connections temporarily.
Add alerts on postgres‑orders CPU >80% and active_connections >150; add Redis memory‑eviction alert.
actions.rationale: Early detection for similar overload patterns.

actions.description: Update change‑management policy for memory‑related GUCs (work_mem) to require canary rollout and post‑change monitoring.
Validate read‑replica fail‑over readiness for postgres‑orders.
actions.rationale: Responder asked about fail‑over; improves resilience.

open_questions: Did Redis experience a restart or OOM around 10:12?
What was the exact request rate on orders‑service at the onset?
Does the positions table have an index on account_id, and are statistics up to date?
Was any feature flag or batch job enabled at 10:10‑10:15 that could cause the query surge?
